package.description:
How do taste buds work, why is the tongue map a myth, and why do your taste cells get replaced about every 10 days? A simple explainer of papillae, taste receptors, the five basic tastes (sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami), why smell makes most of flavor, and the catfish with 175,000 taste buds.

package.pinned_comment: Were you taught the tongue map in school? Tell me which flavor you were told lives on the tip!
package.script: Your taste buds die every ten days, and nobody ever told you why. Right now, thousands of tiny sensors are tasting your own spit. So what are they, how do they work, and what about that tongue map from school? Let's start with the map. You've probably seen it. Sweet on the tip, bitter at the back, sour and salty on the sides. It's a myth. In nineteen oh one, a German scientist named David Hanig found that some spots were just a tiny bit more sensitive. Then in nineteen forty two, his graph got redrawn, and people read it the wrong way. The truth? Every part of your tongue that has taste buds can taste all five flavors. So where are the taste buds? Stick out your tongue in a mirror. Those little bumps are not taste buds. They're called papillae, and most taste buds hide inside them, along the sides of each bump. An adult has somewhere between two thousand and ten thousand taste buds. A few even live on the roof of your mouth and down in your throat. Now zoom in on one bud. It looks a bit like a tiny onion, packed with fifty to one hundred fifty taste cells. At the top there's a little opening, called a taste pore. When you eat, food dissolves in your spit, and those molecules slip into the pore. Each taste cell has receptors on its tip, like locks waiting for the right key. Sugar fits the sweet lock. Salt slips through its own little channel. When a key fits, the cell fires a signal down a nerve, and your brain says, sweet! And here's the clever part. Each of the five tastes has a job. Sweet means energy. Salty means minerals your body needs. Sour can mean unripe, or spoiled. Bitter is a warning, because lots of poisons taste bitter. And umami means protein. That fifth taste was found in nineteen oh eight, by a Japanese chemist named Kikunae Ikeda. He wondered why seaweed soup tasted so rich, and found the answer was glutamate. But taste is only half the story. Hold your nose and eat a jelly bean. You can tell it's sweet, but not what flavor it is. That's because most of what we call flavor actually comes from smell. And some animals put us to shame. A catfish can have up to one hundred seventy five thousand taste buds, all over its body. It's basically a swimming tongue. Now, back to that hook. Your taste cells work in a wet, rough place, getting scraped by crunchy food, and burned by hot soup. So your body replaces them, about every ten days. That's why a burned tongue feels normal again so fast. Every bite you take, thousands of brand new taste cells are on the job. Next time, why do some people get carsick, while others feel totally fine?
key_facts: Adults have about 2,000 to 10,000 taste buds, each with 50 to 150 taste receptor cells; taste cells are replaced roughly every 10 days (Cleveland Clinic)
Most taste buds sit in papillae (fungiform, circumvallate, foliate); a few are on the roof of the mouth and in the throat (Cleveland Clinic)
Tongue map myth: David P. Hanig's 1901 paper found only minute threshold differences; Edwin Boring's 1942 redrawn graphs were misread; all tastes are sensed across the tongue (Wikipedia: Tongue map)
Umami identified by chemist Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 from kombu seaweed broth; the molecule is glutamate (BrainFacts)
Large catfish can have up to 175,000 taste buds, all over the body (Live Science)

package.script: A 500-kilo horse can sleep standing up, and you'd never guess why it doesn't fall. The trick is called the stay apparatus. Tendons and ligaments brace its legs, so the joints lock with almost no muscle effort. In a back leg, the kneecap hooks over a bump on the thigh bone, like a latch clicking shut. The other back leg gets to rest, and every so often it swaps sides. But there's a catch. Dreaming sleep, called REM, relaxes every muscle, and that unlocks the legs. So for REM, a horse has to lie down, about thirty to forty-five minutes a day, often while a buddy stands guard. Miss it for a week or so, and its knees can buckle mid-nap. So, could you sleep standing up, or would you fall flat on your face?

package.script:
A tick glues itself into your skin in thirty minutes,
and you never feel it.
First, two tiny scissor blades
snip a hole in your skin.
Then it slides in a spear called the hypostome,
covered in barbs that point backwards,
like a fishhook.
Once it's in, it won't slide back out.
Now the wild part.
Within minutes,
some ticks start oozing saliva
that hardens into cement,
a little cone of glue around the spear.
And that spit carries a painkiller,
so you don't notice a thing.
It can hang on for a week or more,
and some females swell up
to a hundred times their size.
When it's full,
it breaks free from its own glue in a minute or two,
and drops off.
So which grip is scarier,
the barbs or the glue?

topic.title: Why do some people get carsick and others don't?

package.title: Why Do 1 in 3 People Get Carsick? 🚗
package.description:
Why do some people get carsick while others can read in the back seat? Motion sickness explained in simple words: how your eyes and inner ear (the vestibular system) disagree, the poison theory, the genes behind it, and why the driver almost never feels sick.

Sources:
https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/motion-sickness/
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4383869/
https://www.popsci.com/science/why-people-get-motion-sickness/

package.pinned_comment: Do you get carsick, or are you the one reading a book in the back seat? 🚗
package.script: Every time you get carsick, your brain thinks you've swallowed poison. And for one in three people, that alarm goes off on almost every ride. So why does the back seat wreck some of us, while others read a whole book and feel totally fine? To find out, we need to look inside your head. You know how you're moving using two main systems. Your eyes are one. The other is hidden deep inside each ear. It's called the vestibular system, and it's basically a built-in motion sensor. Three tiny loops filled with fluid sense every time your head turns. And two little sacs lined with tiny crystals feel you speed up, slow down and tip. Most of the time your eyes and ears agree. But picture yourself in the back seat, reading a phone. Your eyes see a screen that isn't moving. Your inner ear feels every bump and every curve. One says still. The other says moving. Scientists call this sensory conflict, and it's the leading explanation for motion sickness. So why would a mixed-up signal make you feel sick? One popular theory goes way back to our ancestors. Long ago, if your senses suddenly stopped agreeing, a likely cause was something toxic you'd eaten. So the brain may have learned a simple rule. Signals don't match? Empty the stomach. Researchers still debate this idea, but it would explain why a bumpy ride can feel a lot like food poisoning. Here's where it gets personal. In 2015 the genetics company 23andMe studied more than eighty thousand people. They found thirty-five spots in our DNA linked to motion sickness. And some studies suggest up to seventy percent of the difference between people comes down to genes. Age matters too. Kids between about seven and twelve get it the most, and lots of people grow out of the worst of it. Women report it more often than men, and so do people who get migraines. So if your whole family turns green on road trips, that's probably not a coincidence. Now for the strangest part. People who have completely lost the motion sensors in their inner ears basically don't get motion sick at all. No inner ear signal, no conflict, no alarm. What you can see matters too. One study found that passengers who couldn't see the road ahead were about three times more likely to feel sick. And the driver? Usually fine. The driver knows every turn before it happens, so the brain isn't caught by surprise. This old alarm is now facing brand new problems. Virtual reality flips the conflict around. Your eyes see motion, but your body sits perfectly still. And as cars start driving themselves, everyone becomes a passenger, staring at screens instead of the road. So engineers are testing tricks, like lights that hint at the next turn, to help your eyes and ears agree again. So the next time a car ride makes you queasy, remember, your brain isn't broken. It's just protecting you from a poison that isn't there. Next time, what really happens if a porcupine's quills get stuck in you?
key_facts: About 1 in 3 people are highly susceptible to motion sickness (MedlinePlus; Hromatka et al. 2015)
The leading explanation is sensory conflict: eyes signal still while the inner ear signals moving
One theory: the brain treats the mismatch like a sign of poisoning and triggers nausea (debated)
A 2015 23andMe study of 80,494 people found 35 genetic variants linked to motion sickness
Heritability estimates for motion sickness range up to about 70%
Children about 7-12 are most susceptible; it is more common in women and in people with migraines
People with complete loss of vestibular function are essentially immune to motion sickness
Passengers without a view of the road ahead were about 3 times more likely to get sick

package.title: Why Does Garlic Breath Last 24 Hours? 🧄

package.script:
Your garlic breath can leak out of your lungs for twenty-four hours. Why?
Mouthwash won't stop it.
Crush a clove of garlic
and it lets off a bunch of stinky sulfur gases.
Most break down fast.
But one is sneaky.
It's called allyl methyl sulfide.
Your gut and liver barely touch it,
so it slips into your blood
and rides around your whole body.
Each time that blood passes through your lungs,
a little leaks out on your breath.
Some even sneaks out through your sweat.
Three hours after dinner,
it's the main garlic smell you're breathing out.
And it keeps that up for hours and hours.
Raw apple, mint or milk can help a little.
So really,
garlic breath is garlic blood.

package.script:
Birds in a V can cut their heart rate 14 percent,
and you've never seen why.
It's the secret behind every V of geese.
Each flap pushes air down behind the wing.
But at the wingtip, air curls up and around,
into a spinning swirl.
Just outside that swirl, the air is rising.
So the bird behind slides into that exact spot,
and gets free lift on every flap.
Line everyone up like that,
and you get a V.
Pelicans tracked in formation
had heart rates up to 14 percent lower than flying solo.
Ibises even time their flaps to match the bird ahead.
But the front bird gets no free ride.
So ibises take turns,
swapping the tiring spot at the front.
Honestly, that's teamwork with zero meetings.
So which bird would you rather be,
the leader at the front, or the one in the back?

A porcupine carries 30,000 tiny harpoons.
So what happens when one sticks into you?
And why won't it come back out?
Let's take a really close look at the pointiest coat in nature.
First, let's bust the biggest myth.
Porcupines can't shoot their quills.
Not even a little.
People have believed it since ancient Greece,
but it just isn't true.
A North American porcupine wears about 30,000 quills
on its back, sides and tail.
Each one is a stiff, hollow hair,
made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails.
They're up to four inches long,
and they're only loosely attached to the skin.
So the porcupine doesn't throw anything.
An attacker bumps into it,
the quills grab hold,
and they pull straight out of the porcupine.
Now let's zoom in on the very tip of one quill.
Under a microscope, it's covered in hundreds of tiny barbs,
all pointing backwards, like the scales on a pine cone.
In 2012, scientists pushed quills into meat in the lab.
The barbs did something surprising.
They cut the force needed to go in by about half.
The tiny barbs grip the tissue and slice it,
a bit like the teeth on a bread knife.
So the quill slides in deep and easy.
Then they tried pulling them out.
Now the barbs flare open and snag,
and it took about four times more force
than a smooth quill.
In, easy. Out, really hard.
Just like a fishhook.
Less than half a centimeter in,
and it's already holding on.
And here's the sneaky part.
A quill that's stuck doesn't just sit there.
Every time the animal moves,
its own muscles squeeze around the barbs,
and each one can only ratchet one way.
Forward.
So a stuck quill slowly works its way deeper.
That's why a dog that noses a porcupine
needs a trip to the vet, and fast.
But here's the thing.
A porcupine would much rather not fight at all.
It gives you plenty of warning first.
It growls.
It chatters its teeth.
It raises its black and white quills
like a giant pincushion.
And it releases a smell from a patch on its lower back.
One scientist said it smells a bit like goat,
or a strange, stinky cheese.
If you still don't back off,
it turns around and swings its tail.
Thwack.
And there's one more twist.
Porcupines sometimes stab themselves,
like when they fall out of a tree.
So their quills come coated in greasy fats
that fight off germs.
Built-in antibiotic.
Scientists love these quills.
The same team that tested the barbs
is copying them for medical needles and staples
that slide in gently
and hold on tight.
So a porcupine's quill is a hair
that works like a fishhook,
goes in easy, comes out hard,
and keeps itself clean.
Not bad for a hair.
Next time, how does a homing pigeon
find its way home from hundreds of miles away?

00:00:15,010 --> 00:00:17,040
Porcupines can't shoot their quills.

7
00:00:17,390 --> 00:00:18,490
Not even a little.

8
00:00:18,770 --> 00:00:21,180
People have believed it since ancient Greece,

9
00:00:21,550 --> 00:00:22,840
but it just isn't true.

10
00:00:23,220 --> 00:00:27,060
A North American porcupine wears about 30,000 quills

11
00:00:27,130 --> 00:00:29,160
on its back, sides and tail.

12
00:00:29,530 --> 00:00:32,040
Each one is a stiff, hollow hair,

13
00:00:32,100 --> 00:00:35,130
made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails.

14
00:00:35,490 --> 00:00:37,020
They're up to four inches long,

15
00:00:37,420 --> 00:00:39,810
and they're only loosely attached to the skin.

16
00:00:40,270 --> 00:00:42,360
So the porcupine doesn't throw anything.

17
00:00:42,710 --> 00:00:44,100
An attacker bumps into it,

18
00:00:44,410 --> 00:00:45,820
the quills grab hold,

19
00:00:46,210 --> 00:00:48,200
and they pull straight out of the porcupine.

20
00:00:48,650 --> 00:00:51,750
Now let's zoom in on the very tip of one quill.

21
00:00:52,230 --> 00:00:55,950
Under a microscope, it's covered in hundreds of tiny barbs,

22
00:00:56,360 --> 00:01:00,140
all pointing backwards, like the scales on a pine cone.

23
00:01:00,590 --> 00:01:04,880
In 2012, scientists pushed quills into meat in the lab.

24
00:01:05,220 --> 00:01:07,200
The barbs did something surprising.

25
00:01:07,670 --> 00:01:10,750
They cut the force needed to go in by about half.

26
00:01:11,220 --> 00:01:13,880
The tiny barbs grip the tissue and slice it,

27
00:01:14,360 --> 00:01:16,570
a bit like the teeth on a bread knife.

28
00:01:16,990 --> 00:01:19,220
So the quill slides in deep and easy.

29
00:01:19,680 --> 00:01:21,250
Then they tried pulling them out.

30
00:01:21,680 --> 00:01:23,770
Now the barbs flare open and snag,

31
00:01:24,340 --> 00:01:26,480
and it took about four times more force

32
00:01:26,540 --> 00:01:27,590
than a smooth quill.

33
00:01:27,980 --> 00:01:30,040
In, easy. Out, really hard.

34
00:01:30,520 --> 00:01:31,720
Just like a fishhook.

35
00:01:32,020 --> 00:01:33,830
Less than half a centimeter in,

36
00:01:34,210 --> 00:01:35,600
and it's already holding on.

37
00:01:36,080 --> 00:01:37,570
And here's the sneaky part.

38
00:01:37,970 --> 00:01:40,110
A quill that's stuck doesn't just sit there.

39
00:01:40,460 --> 00:01:42,230
Every time the animal moves,

40
00:01:42,660 --> 00:01:45,130
its own muscles squeeze around the barbs,

41
00:01:45,550 --> 00:01:47,890
and each one can only ratchet one way.

42
00:01:48,260 --> 00:01:49,040
Forward.

43
00:01:49,420 --> 00:01:52,060
So a stuck quill slowly works its way deeper.

44
00:01:52,440 --> 00:01:54,930
That's why a dog that noses a porcupine

45
00:01:55,330 --> 00:01:57,410
needs a trip to the vet, and fast.

46
00:01:57,810 --> 00:01:58,910
But here's the thing.

47
00:01:59,230 --> 00:02:01,940
A porcupine would much rather not fight at all.

48
00:02:02,360 --> 00:02:04,450
It gives you plenty of warning first.

49
00:02:04,830 --> 00:02:05,700
It growls.

50
00:02:05,990 --> 00:02:07,270
It chatters its teeth.

51
00:02:07,620 --> 00:02:09,820
It raises its black and white quills

52
00:02:10,090 --> 00:02:11,390
like a giant pincushion.

53
00:02:11,810 --> 00:02:14,590
And it releases a smell from a patch on its lower back.

54
00:02:15,030 --> 00:02:17,360
One scientist said it smells a bit like goat,

55
00:02:17,890 --> 00:02:19,780
or a strange, stinky cheese.

56
00:02:20,160 --> 00:02:21,540
If you still don't back off,

57
00:02:21,890 --> 00:02:23,990
it turns around and swings its tail.

58
00:02:24,390 --> 00:02:25,030
Thwack.

59
00:02:25,320 --> 00:02:26,760
And there's one more twist.

60
00:02:27,170 --> 00:02:29,510
Porcupines sometimes stab themselves,

61
00:02:29,890 --> 00:02:31,510
like when they fall out of a tree.

62
00:02:31,910 --> 00:02:34,990
So their quills come coated in greasy fats

63
00:02:35,050 --> 00:02:35,680
that fight off germs.

64
00:02:36,130 --> 00:02:37,770
Built-in antibiotic.

65
00:02:38,080 --> 00:02:39,840
Scientists love these quills.

66
00:02:40,130 --> 00:02:42,160
The same team that tested the barbs

67

is copying them for medical needles and staples

68

that slide in gently

69
00:02:46,990 --> 00:02:48,130
and hold on tight.

70
00:02:48,580 --> 00:02:50,730
So a porcupine's quill is a hair

71
00:02:50,730 --> 00:02:52,870
that works like a fishhook,

72
00:02:52,970 --> 00:02:54,530
goes in easy, comes out hard,

73
00:02:54,530 --> 00:02:56,170
and keeps itself clean.

74
00:02:56,600 --> 00:02:57,850
Not bad for a hair.

Next time, how does a homing pigeon

find its way home from hundreds of miles away?

topic.title: Why do zebras have stripes?

package.title: Why Do Zebras Have Stripes? 🦓
package.description:
Why do zebras have stripes? Scientists filmed biting horseflies around zebras and horses and found the flies landed on zebras less than a quarter as often, because the stripes seem to stop them braking for a landing.

Sources:
https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2019/02/190220145032.htm
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/scientists-dressed-horses-zebras-determine-purpose-stripes-180971540/

package.pinned_comment: Would you wear stripes to a picnic to keep the flies off? Yes or no?
package.script:
Zebra stripes stop 3 out of 4 fly landings,
and you can see why.
In Africa, biting horseflies swarm grazing animals,
and their bites can spread nasty diseases.
So researchers in Britain filmed flies
buzzing around zebras and horses.
The flies flew up to both just as often.
But they landed on zebras less than a quarter as often.
So what's going on?
Near a horse, a fly slows down for a soft landing.
Near a zebra, the stripes seem to scramble its eyes,
so it never brakes,
and it bumps right off or zooms past.
Then they dressed horses in striped coats.
Flies kept missing the coats,
but still landed on their bare heads.
Honestly, that's kind of genius.
Camouflage? Keeping cool? The evidence for those is weaker.
So would you wear stripes to your next picnic?
key_facts: Horseflies approached zebras and horses at similar rates (Caro et al., PLOS ONE 2019)
Flies landed on zebras less than a quarter as often as on horses
Flies failed to slow down near zebras and bumped into them or flew past
Horses wearing striped coats got far fewer landings on the coat but not on their bare heads
Study done on a farm in Britain; camouflage and cooling ideas have weaker support

topic.title: What's really inside a camel's hump?

package.title: What's Really Inside a Camel's Hump? 🐪
package.description:
What's inside a camel's hump? Not water: a dromedary's hump stores up to about 35 kg of fat for energy, while its water is spread through its whole body, it can lose about a quarter of its weight in water, and then drink around 100 litres in roughly ten minutes thanks to oval red blood cells that can swell without bursting.

https://www.clevelandzoosociety.org/z/2021/04/06/truth-or-tail-a-camels-hump

package.script: A camel's hump hides up to 35 kilos of fat, not a drop of water. Here's why you never knew. Fat is food in a backpack. When there's nothing to eat, the camel burns that fat for energy, and the hump shrinks and flops over. With all the fat in one lump, the rest of the body stays lean and cool. Okay, so where's the water? It's spread through the whole body. A camel can lose a quarter of its weight in water and keep walking. Its oval blood cells keep sliding along even as its blood thickens. Then it finds a well, and drinks around a hundred litres in about ten minutes. Those blood cells swell to twice their size without bursting. So if you had a hump, what would you store in yours?

topic.title: What is the crusty 'sleep' in your eyes?

package.title: Eye Crust: What Happens When 14,000 Blinks Stop 👁️
package.description:
What is the crusty 'sleep' in your eyes every morning? Eye crust, or rheum, is mucus, oil, dust and dead skin cells that your blinks normally wash away, but when you sleep the blinking stops, so it collects in the corners of your eyes and dries out.

Sources:
https://health.clevelandclinic.org/why-your-eyes-are-crusty-in-the-morning/
https://www.healthline.com/health/how-many-times-do-you-blink-a-day

Animated in the Kawaii Anime style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
package.pinned_comment: What do YOU call it: sleep, eye boogers, or crust? Or something else?
package.script:
You wake up with dead skin glued in your eyes.
Why?
All day, your eyes wear a thin film of tears,
made of water, sticky mucus and a little oil.
Dust and old skin cells get trapped in it.
But you blink about 15 to 20 times a minute.
That's over 14,000 blinks a day,
and every blink washes that gunk away.
Then you fall asleep,
and the blinking stops.
Now the mucus, oil, dust and dead skin have nowhere to go.
They drift into the corners of your eyes,
and overnight they dry out
into crusty little flakes.
Doctors call it rheum.
And a little every morning is totally normal.
Honestly, it's just yesterday's cleanup, waiting for you.
So what do you call it: sleep, eye boogers, or crust?
key_facts: Eye crust (rheum) is mucus, oil, dirt and skin cells that collect in the corners of the eyes (Cleveland Clinic)
During the day frequent blinking washes them away; asleep you don't blink, so they accumulate and dry into crust (Cleveland Clinic)
Most people blink 15-20 times a minute, about 14,400-19,200 times a day while awake (Healthline)
The tear film is made of water, mucus and oil
A little morning crust is normal (Cleveland Clinic)

topic.title: Why do cats knead with their paws?

package.title: Why Does Your Cat Knead You? 🐾
package.description:
Why do cats knead? Kneading, or making biscuits, starts when nursing kittens press their paws on their mother to get milk flowing, and many adult cats keep doing it when they feel safe and calm, while scent glands between their paw pads leave a smell that marks you as theirs.

Sources:
https://www.livescience.com/animals/cats/why-do-cats-knead
https://www.petmd.com/cat/behavior/why-do-cats-knead
https://vcahospitals.com/resources/behavior-cat/true-or-false-do-cats-knead

package.pinned_comment: When your cat kneads you, is it being a kitten again, or stamping you as its property?
package.script: Why does your cat knead you? It's a kitten trick it never quit. Newborn kittens can barely see, but they can push. They press tiny front paws into their mom, left, right, left, and that gets the milk flowing. Push, push, sip. Most cats just never outgrow it. Grown cats knead when they feel safe and calm, so a cat kneading your lap is kind of a big compliment. But there's a sneaky second job. Cats have scent glands between their paw pads. Every push leaves a smell you can't notice, but other cats can. It's like a tiny stamp that says, mine. Wild cats even knead soft grass to make a comfy bed before a nap. So when your cat kneads you, is it being a kitten again, or stamping you as its property?
key_facts: Nursing kittens knead their mother to stimulate milk flow (Live Science, PetMD)
Many adult cats knead when they feel safe and relaxed (Live Science, PetMD)
Cats have scent glands between their paw pads; kneading may mark territory (PetMD, VCA)

package.title: How Do Pigeons Fly 600 Miles Home?
package.description:
Homing pigeons can find their loft from hundreds of miles away using a sun compass, a magnetic sense on cloudy days, a smell map carried on the wind, and roads and landmarks for the last few miles. We look at William Keeton's clock-shift trick that sent pigeons 90 degrees off course, the tiny magnets that got them lost under clouds, the Oxford GPS study that caught pigeons following highways and roundabouts, and how fast racing pigeons really fly.

package.pinned_comment: Which sense surprised you most: the sun compass, the magnetic backup, the smell map or the roads?
package.script:
Take a pigeon six hundred miles from home and let it go.
It'll be back the same day.
No map, no phone, no GPS.
And nobody fully knows how it does it.
So how does a bird that small know the way?
Let's take a ride along its route.
People figured out this trick a long time ago.
The ancient Egyptians and Romans carried pigeons on trips
and let them go with messages.
Back in 44 BC, a Roman general sent his notes by pigeon.
Here's the secret.
Any pigeon can find its own home.
Breeders just start them young,
with short practice flights from a mile or two away,
then farther and farther.
Scientists think a pigeon needs two tools.
A compass, to tell which way is which.
And a map, to know where home actually is.
Let's start with the compass.
On a sunny day, a pigeon steers by the sun.
But the sun moves fifteen degrees every hour,
so the bird has to know what time it is.
Decades ago, a scientist named William Keeton played a sneaky trick.
He kept pigeons under lamps that ran six hours off.
Then he let them go on a sunny day.
Home was west,
but the birds flew north.
They were off by ninety degrees,
exactly what a six-hour mistake would cause.
So the sun really is their compass.
But what about cloudy days?
Pigeons still get home.
Keeton tried tiny magnets on their backs.
In sunshine, the magnets did nothing.
Under clouds, those birds got lost.
So pigeons have a backup.
They can feel Earth's magnetic field.
A compass is great,
but it's useless if you don't know where home is.
So where's the map?
Many scientists think it's up the pigeon's nose.
Pigeons that can't smell
get lost when they're released somewhere new.
The idea is that every region has its own mix of smells,
carried along by the wind.
A young pigeon sitting in its loft
learns which smells blow in from which direction.
Smell the forest, and home is that way.
Some researchers think pigeons might also hear
super-low sounds that travel for miles,
but that's still being tested.
Now here's the funniest part.
Close to home, pigeons switch to their eyes.
Oxford scientists put tiny GPS trackers on pigeons.
And the birds followed the roads.
They flew straight down a highway,
turned at the traffic lights,
and even went around a roundabout.
It's easier than thinking, so they just follow the road.
So how good are they?
A racing pigeon averages about fifty miles an hour.
With a tailwind, it can hit ninety.
Some races run six hundred miles,
and the longest have gone over a thousand miles.
Sun for the compass.
Magnetism when it's cloudy.
Smell for the map.
And roads for the last few miles.
Four senses, one tiny brain, and it still beats your phone's battery.
Next time, your bones are alive.
So how do they rebuild themselves?

Races commonly run up to about 600 miles; the longest races are around 1,100 miles (CBS Minnesota; EarthDate)
Pigeons were used as messengers in ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome; pigeon post was used at the siege of Modena in 44 BC (EarthDate)
Young birds are trained with short releases that get gradually farther from the loft
The sun moves about 15 degrees an hour; a 6-hour clock shift sends pigeons about 90 degrees off (Keeton 1969; textbook ch. 45.4)
Pigeons wearing magnets home fine on sunny days but fail on cloudy days (Keeton; textbook ch. 45.4)
Pigeons that cannot smell cannot navigate from unfamiliar places; the map is thought to be olfactory, built from wind-borne odours (The Conversation; Wallraff 2013 via ScienceDaily)
Infrasound has been proposed as a cue but has little support so far (The Conversation; EarthDate)
Oxford GPS tracking (Guilford) showed pigeons following roads such as the A34, turning at traffic lights and going around roundabouts (AFP via Al Jazeera, 2004)

package.script:
Why does a banana get brown spots?
You'd never guess it's on purpose.
It starts with a gas called ethylene.
The banana makes it all by itself,
and it flips ripening on like a switch.
First, the green chlorophyll in the peel breaks down,
so the yellow underneath finally shows.
Inside, starch turns into sugar.
Sugar can climb from about 1 percent to around 17.
Then the peel starts getting old.
Little clusters of cells shut down on schedule,
and an enzyme called polyphenol oxidase
links chemicals in the peel into brown pigment.
That's your spot.
And here's the wild part.
Under ultraviolet light,
each spot glows with a bright blue ring,
from leftover bits of chlorophyll.
So more spots usually means a sweeter banana.
Which one do you grab:
green, yellow, or totally spotty?

package.script:
Why can't you stop yourself from catching a yawn?
Even reading the word yawn can set one off.
You might be fighting one right now.
Seeing, hearing, or just thinking about a yawn
can trigger your own.
In one Duke study,
three hundred twenty eight people watched a three minute video of yawns.
Two hundred twenty two of them yawned too.
That's about two out of three!
And who's yawning matters.
An Italian study found yawns spread fastest between family,
then friends,
and slowest between strangers.
So some scientists link it to empathy,
your brain quietly copying the people you care about.
Little kids don't catch yawns until they're about four.
But your dog can catch yours.

package.title: You Get a New Skeleton Every 10 Years
package.description:
Your bones are living tissue: you're born with nearly 300 bones that fuse down to about 206, and cells called osteoclasts and osteoblasts dig out and rebuild about 10% of your skeleton every year. package.pinned_comment: Did you know you were born with nearly 300 bones? Which fact surprised you most: the fusing bones, the new skeleton every 10 years, or the 200 billion blood cells a day?
package.script:
You were born with nearly three hundred bones.
So where did almost a hundred of them go?
The answer is that your skeleton is alive,
and it's rebuilding itself right now.
Most of us picture bones as dry white sticks,
like the plastic skeleton in a science class.
But the bones inside you have blood vessels,
nerves, and billions of busy cells.
So what's actually going on in there?
Let's paint it out, one bone at a time.
Chapter one. More bones than you think.
A grown-up has about two hundred and six bones.
But a newborn has close to three hundred.
The missing ones didn't disappear.
They fused together as you grew.
A baby's skull is a set of soft plates,
with gaps that slowly close and lock.
Five little bones at the bottom of your spine
join up into one solid piece.
Your hands and feet hold one hundred and six bones,
more than half of your whole skeleton.
Chapter two. What bone is made of.
Bone is a mix of two very different things.
The first is collagen,
a stretchy protein, a bit like rope.
The second is a hard mineral made of calcium,
packed between the ropes like tiny bricks.
Rope alone would bend, bricks alone would shatter.
Together, you get something tough and a little springy.
And your bones are also a bank.
They store about ninety nine percent of your body's calcium.
When your blood runs low,
your bones pay some out,
so your heart and muscles keep working.
Chapter three. The demolition crew.
Deep inside every bone, two kinds of cells take turns.
Osteoclasts dissolve tiny pockets of old bone.
Then osteoblasts move in,
and fill the hole with fresh new bone.
Dig, then fill. Dig, then fill.
In adults, around ten percent of the skeleton
gets rebuilt every year.
That works out to roughly a brand new skeleton
about every ten years.
This same crew is why a broken bone can heal.
First a soft bridge forms across the crack,
then the crew slowly turns it into hard bone again.
Chapter four. The blood factory.
Now look inside a big bone, like your thigh bone.
The middle is filled with soft marrow,
and that marrow is a factory.
It makes your red blood cells,
the white cells that fight germs,
and the platelets that plug up cuts.
How many? Scientists estimate
around two hundred billion red blood cells,
every single day.
Chapter five. Use it or lose it.
Your bones listen to how you use them.
Push on them, and they build up.
Rest them for too long, and they let go.
Astronauts floating in space can lose
about one percent of the bone in their hips each month.
Meanwhile, studies of tennis players find
the bones in their racket arm are thicker
than the bones in their other arm.
So every jump, every run, every climb up the stairs
is a little message telling your skeleton to stay strong.
So no, your skeleton isn't a dead frame.
It's a living, growing part of you,
quietly rebuilding itself, one tiny pocket at a time.
Next time, your liver,
the organ that does hundreds of jobs at once.
key_facts: Adults have about 206 bones; newborns have close to 300, many of which fuse during growth (Healthline; Popular Science)
A baby's skull plates are separated by sutures and soft spots (fontanelles) that close as the child grows
Five sacral vertebrae fuse into the sacrum
Hands (27 bones each) and feet (26 each) together hold 106 of the 206 bones
Bone is collagen (protein) plus calcium phosphate mineral (hydroxyapatite); it stores about 99% of the body's calcium
Osteoclasts resorb bone, osteoblasts form new bone; about 10% of the adult skeleton is remodeled each year, roughly a new skeleton every 10 years (Surgeon General's report, NBK45504)
Fractures heal via a soft callus that is remodeled into hard bone
Bone marrow makes red cells, white cells and platelets; around 200 billion red blood cells per day (The Blood Project)
Astronauts can lose about 1-1.5% of hip and spine bone mass per month in microgravity (NASA)
Tennis players' racket-arm bones are thicker/denser than the other arm (loading studies)

package.title: Polar Bears Aren't White (0 White Hairs) 🐻‍❄️
package.description:
Why do polar bears have black skin under white fur? Polar bear hairs are clear and hollow with no white pigment, and they only look white because light scatters inside them, while most warmth comes from thick fat and fur that traps heat so well polar bears almost vanish on heat cameras.

package.pinned_comment: So is a polar bear white, black, or totally see-through? Pick one 👇
package.script: If you shaved a polar bear, you'd find black skin. And zero white hairs. Why? Each hair is clear, like a tiny plastic straw with a hollow core full of air. There's no white pigment in it. So why does it look white? Light bounces around inside those clear hairs and scatters in every direction, the same trick that makes snow look white. Scientists once thought the hairs piped sunlight down to the skin like fiber optics. Turns out they don't. Most sunlight never reaches the skin. The black skin may soak up what little warmth gets through, but the real heater is underneath: up to eleven centimeters of fat, plus fur that traps heat so well polar bears almost vanish on heat cameras. So is a polar bear white, black, or totally see-through?

topic.title: Why do your ears and nose seem to keep growing as you age?

package.title: Your Ears Get 0.22 mm Longer Every Year 👂

package.pinned_comment: How much longer will your ears be at 100? Do the math and drop your guess 👇
package.script: Your ears never stop getting longer, but they aren't growing. Your nose droops lower every year too. So what's stretching them? Your bones stopped getting longer years ago. The floppy parts of your ears and nose are cartilage and skin, held up by springy fibers called collagen and elastin. As you get older, your body makes fewer of those fibers. The springs get weaker, and gravity wins. Every single year it pulls them down a tiny bit more. Earlobes stretch the most, because there's no cartilage inside them at all. Just skin and fat. One study of two hundred and six adults found ears get about zero point two two millimeters longer every year after age thirty. That's roughly a whole centimeter by eighty. So nothing's growing. Your face is just slowly sagging. So how much longer will your ears be at a hundred?

topic.title: The Cheetah Paradox: why can the fastest land animal only sprint for about 20 seconds?

package.title: Why Cheetahs Quit After 20 Seconds 🐆
package.description:
Why does a cheetah, the fastest land animal at about 100 km/h, give up a chase after roughly 20 seconds? It isn't overheating: a 2013 study that put sensors on six hunting cheetahs found their body temperature barely changed during the sprint, so the real limit is how fast that springy, all-out gallop burns energy.

Sources:
https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/its-a-myth-that-cheetahs-overheat-while-hunting
https://nationalzoo.si.edu/animals/cheetah
https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2013.0472

Animated in the Low-Poly Faceted style.

package.pinned_comment: Would you rather be cheetah-fast for 20 seconds, or slower all day? 🐆
package.script: A cheetah quits after twenty seconds, and you'd never guess why. It hits about a hundred kilometers an hour, zero to seventy-two in two and a half seconds. Each stride covers seven meters, four strides every second. Its spine bends like a spring, its lungs and heart are huge, and its tail steers like a rudder. People thought it stopped because it overheated. But in 2013, scientists put sensors on six cheetahs. During the chase, body heat barely changed. It only jumped after a catch, probably from stress, with lions nearby. So what stops them? That springy sprint burns energy crazy fast, so a full sprint lasts about twenty seconds, just a few hundred meters. Miss by then, and the cheetah's done. Only about half its chases end in a meal. Would you rather be that fast for twenty seconds, or slower all day?

topic.title: Why are babies born without hard kneecaps?

package.title: Babies Have No Bony Kneecaps (Until Age 3) 🦵
package.description:
Why are babies born without bony kneecaps? A baby's kneecap starts as soft cartilage and only begins turning to bone between about ages 3 and 6, fusing into one solid kneecap by the early teens.

Sources:
https://www.healthline.com/health/do-babies-have-kneecaps
https://radiopaedia.org/articles/24732

Animated in the Flat-Vector Science style.

package.pinned_comment: Be honest: did you know you were born without bony kneecaps? 🦵
package.script: Your kneecaps were soft until you were about three. Babies don't have bony kneecaps at all. Each knee has a soft disc of cartilage instead, the same bendy stuff in the tip of your nose. So why start soft? First, there's birth itself. A hard kneecap would make that tight squeeze riskier. Then comes crawling. Knees hit the floor again and again, and soft cartilage handles that better than bone. Then somewhere between ages three and six, tiny islands of bone pop up inside the cartilage. They grow, they spread, and by your early teens they've fused into one solid kneecap. And honestly, it's kind of a weird bone. It's the biggest bone in your body that grows right inside a tendon. That's why a toddler's knees are still so squishy. So be honest. Did you know you were born without kneecaps?

Patella ossification centers appear between about 3 and 6 years (Radiopaedia; Healthline says 2-6)
Several pieces harden and fuse into one bone by about age 10-12 / puberty
A rigid kneecap could make birth harder; cartilage handles crawling and learning to walk better (Healthline)
The patella is the largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon (Radiopaedia)

topic.title: Your Liver Explained in Simple Words: the organ that does hundreds of jobs

package.title: Your Liver Can Regrow 2/3 of Itself in Weeks
package.description:
Your liver is your biggest internal organ and does more than 500 jobs: it filters your blood, turns toxic ammonia into urea, makes bile to digest fat, stores glycogen, vitamins and iron, and builds clotting proteins. We paint how the liver works, why poop is brown, and how a liver can grow back after up to two thirds is removed, which is what makes living liver donors possible.

Sources:
https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/conditions-and-diseases/liver-anatomy-and-functions
https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/21481-liver
https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/treatments/22930-hepatectomy-liver-resection

Animated in the Watercolor Brush style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
package.pinned_comment: Your liver can lose two thirds of itself and grow back in weeks. Which of its jobs surprised you most: the filter, the bile factory, the pantry, or the regrowing?
package.script:
You could lose two thirds of your liver, and it would actually grow back.
In a few weeks, it's almost back to full size.
No other organ inside you can pull that off.
And while it's doing that, it's still running more than five hundred jobs.
So what is this thing, and how does it do it all?
Let's paint it out, one job at a time.
Chapter one. The biggest organ inside you.
Tuck your hand under your right ribs.
That's roughly where your liver sits.
It's a soft, reddish-brown wedge about the size of a football,
and it weighs around one and a half kilos.
That makes it your biggest internal organ.
And it's always full of blood, about a pint at any moment.
Most of that blood comes straight from your gut,
through one big pipe called the portal vein.
So everything you eat and drink passes through your liver first,
before it reaches the rest of your body.
Chapter two. The filter.
Think of your liver as a security checkpoint.
Inside, it's built from millions of tiny cells called hepatocytes,
lined up in rows like the pages of a book.
Blood seeps slowly between those rows,
and the cells grab anything that shouldn't be there.
Old medicines, leftover chemicals, and alcohol all get broken down here.
Your muscles also make a waste called ammonia,
which is toxic if it builds up.
Your liver turns it into urea,
a much safer waste that your kidneys flush out.
Chapter three. The bile factory.
Your liver also makes bile, a greenish-yellow juice,
up to about a litre of it every day.
Bile works a lot like dish soap.
It breaks big blobs of fat into tiny droplets,
so your gut can actually digest them.
Between meals, the bile waits in a little pouch called the gallbladder.
And here's a weird one.
Bile carries leftovers from old red blood cells,
and that's what turns your poop brown.
Chapter four. The pantry.
After a meal, your liver packs extra sugar away
as a starch called glycogen.
Then, between meals or while you sleep,
it turns that glycogen back into sugar,
so your brain never runs out of fuel.
It also keeps a stash of vitamin A, vitamin D,
vitamin B twelve, and iron, for later.
And it builds proteins your blood needs,
including the ones that make a cut stop bleeding.
Chapter five. The comeback organ.
Now back to that superpower.
Doctors can remove up to two thirds of a healthy liver,
and the rest starts growing right away.
The cells that are left simply divide,
and the liver can get back most of its size in a few weeks.
That's why living donors are possible.
A healthy adult gives part of their liver to someone who needs it,
and both pieces grow into full-size livers.
And scientists are still working out exactly how it knows when to stop.
So the next time you eat a meal,
remember the quiet organ under your ribs,
filtering, storing, building, and regrowing,
more than five hundred jobs, all at once.
Next time, what really happens if you swallow chewing gum?
Does it actually stay inside you for seven years?
key_facts: The liver is the largest internal (solid) organ, about 1.5 kg / 3 lb (Cleveland Clinic)
It performs more than 500 functions (Johns Hopkins Medicine)
It holds about a pint (~13%) of the body's blood at any moment; most of its blood arrives via the portal vein from the gut (Johns Hopkins)
Liver makes bile (roughly up to a litre a day), stored in the gallbladder; bilirubin from old red blood cells gives stool its brown colour
It converts ammonia to urea, stores glycogen, vitamins A, D, B12 and iron, and makes clotting proteins (Johns Hopkins)
Up to two thirds of a healthy liver can be removed; it can regenerate in as little as a few weeks, sometimes several months; in living donation both parts grow back to full size (Cleveland Clinic)

What really happens if you swallow chewing gum? Your body can't digest gum base, but it doesn't need to: swallowed gum moves through your stomach and intestines like corn skins and seeds and usually leaves within a few days, not seven years. package.script:
Swallowed gum never stays in you for seven years.
It's actually gone in a few days.
So where did the seven-year story come from?
And what actually happens to gum inside you?
Let's follow one swallowed piece, all the way through.
Chapter one. The seven-year myth.
Almost everyone hears it as a kid.
Swallow your gum, and it sits in your stomach for seven years.
Nobody really knows who started it.
But there's a grain of truth hiding inside.
Your body can't digest gum. Not properly.
It just doesn't need to.
Chapter two. What gum is made of.
People have chewed gummy stuff for thousands of years.
In Denmark, scientists found a lump of chewed birch tar
about five thousand seven hundred years old.
It still held the chewer's DNA, and her tooth marks.
Far away, the Maya chewed chicle,
a milky sap tapped from the sapodilla tree.
In the eighteen seventies, an inventor named Thomas Adams
started selling chicle as chewing gum in America.
Today most gum starts with a gum base,
made of rubbery, food-grade polymers.
Then sweetener, softeners and flavour get mixed in.
Chapter three. Why you can't digest it.
Digestion is mostly chemistry.
Your spit, stomach and gut make enzymes,
tiny molecular scissors that snip food into pieces.
One kind cuts starch, one cuts protein, and one cuts fat.
The sugar and flavour in gum dissolve away while you chew.
But the gum base is made of long, tangled chains
that none of those scissors can cut.
Even your stomach acid barely touches it.
So the rubbery part stays rubbery, the whole way through.
And honestly, that's fine.
Your body handles stuff it can't digest every single day.
Chapter four. The journey out.
Once you swallow, the gum slides down your food pipe in seconds.
In your stomach, strong muscle walls churn it with your lunch.
Then it squeezes through a little gate at the bottom,
into your small intestine,
a tube roughly six metres long, all folded up.
Waves of muscle push it along, like toothpaste in a tube.
And between meals, your gut runs a cleanup cycle.
Every ninety minutes to two hours or so,
a strong wave sweeps the leftovers onward.
Scientists nicknamed it the housekeeper.
The gum rides along with corn skins, seeds and fibre,
through the large intestine,
and out with everything else, usually within a few days.
Chapter five. When it can go wrong.
So one swallowed piece is no big deal.
But doctors have reported rare cases in young kids
who swallowed gum every day, piece after piece.
The gum clumped together, sometimes with coins or seeds,
into a sticky ball that got stuck.
Those cases are rare, and they took a lot of gum.
So the best place for gum is still the bin, not your belly.
The seven-year myth is wrong,
but it's wrong in an interesting way.
Your body can't break gum down.
It simply moves it along, and shows it the door.
Next time, why are sloths so slow?
And how does being slow keep them alive?

A ~5,700-year-old chewed birch-pitch 'gum' from Syltholm, Denmark yielded a full human genome and oral microbes (Scientific American / Nature Communications 2019)
The Maya and Aztecs chewed chicle, sap from the sapodilla tree (Manilkara zapota); Thomas Adams began selling chicle chewing gum in New York in the early 1870s
Between meals the migrating motor complex sweeps the stomach and small intestine roughly every 90-120 minutes ('housekeeper' wave)
The small intestine is roughly 6 m (about 20 ft) long
Rare gum bezoars have been reported in children who habitually swallowed large amounts of gum, sometimes with coins or seeds (Milov et al., Pediatrics 1998)

topic.title: Why do your teeth chatter when you're cold?

package.title: Why Teeth Chatter: Shivering Makes 5x the Heat 🥶
package.description:
Why do your teeth chatter when you're cold? Your brain's hypothalamus makes your muscles shiver to generate heat, and your small, light, hinged jaw rattles so your teeth click together.

Sources:

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11394237/

package.pinned_comment: When you're freezing, what chatters first: your teeth or your knees? 🥶
package.script: Your chattering teeth mean your brain is burning fuel before you freeze. When your skin senses cold, a spot deep in your brain called the hypothalamus hits the panic button. It can't just crank up a thermostat, so it makes your muscles shiver. Tiny fast squeezes, over and over, and every squeeze burns fuel and leaks heat. At full blast, shivering can make about five times the heat your body makes at rest. Your jaw muscles join in too. But your jaw is small and light, and it hangs on a hinge, so every twitch swings it. Top teeth smack bottom teeth. Click, click, click. Your legs and back are shivering too, they're just too heavy to rattle. And honestly, that's kind of genius. Your body turns its own muscles into a furnace. So be honest. When you're freezing, what chatters first, your teeth or your knees?
key_facts: Shivering is involuntary rapid muscle contraction triggered by the brain (hypothalamus) to make heat (PopSci)
Peak shivering measured at 4.9x resting metabolism; ~5x reported (Eur J Appl Physiol 2001, PubMed 11394237)
Chattering happens because face and jaw muscles shiver too, banging the teeth together (ScienceABC)
Jaw is a light, hinged bone, so its shivering is visible/audible while bigger muscles' shivering isn't (explanatory)

topic.title: Why don't vultures get sick from eating rotten meat?

package.title: Why Vultures Eat Rot: Stomach Acid at pH 1 🦅
package.description:
Why don't vultures get sick from eating rotten meat? Their stomach acid sits close to pH 1 and kills most germs, and the tough gut bacteria that survive, Clostridia and Fusobacteria, help digest the carcass.

Sources:
https://insider.si.edu/2014/11/vultures-remarkably-tolerant-to-deadly-bacteria-study-reveals
https://www.nature.com/news/microbes-help-vultures-eat-rotting-meat-1.16345
https://www.todayifoundout.com/index.php/2014/10/dont-vultures-get-sick-eating-dead-things-cant/

Animated in the Cut-Paper Diorama style.

Follow Zorbly AI for a new Short every day.
package.pinned_comment: Which grosses you out more: the rotten meat, or the gut full of flesh-eating bacteria? 🦅
package.script: Vultures eat rotten meat that would kill you, and never get sick. Why? A carcass can be crawling with germs like anthrax, and the vulture keeps eating. First, the stomach. Vulture stomach acid sits close to pH 1, nearly as strong as battery acid. Most germs die right there. In one study of fifty vultures, scientists found five hundred twenty-eight kinds of bacteria on their faces, but only seventy-six made it to the gut. And the ones that survive? Tough, meat-eating microbes called Clostridia and Fusobacteria, germs that make most other animals sick. In a vulture, they're on the team, helping break down the meal. By cleaning up carcasses, vultures stop those germs from spreading. So be honest. Which grosses you out more, the rotten meat, or the gut full of flesh-eating bacteria?
key_facts: Vulture stomach acid is commonly cited near pH 1, killing most ingested bacteria (Smithsonian Insider: 'extremely harsh chemical environment'; TodayIFoundOut)
2014 Nature Communications study sampled 50 vultures (25 turkey, 25 black) in Tennessee (Smithsonian Insider)
On average 528 microbe types on the face, only 76 in the large intestine (Smithsonian Insider)
Gut dominated by Clostridia and Fusobacteria, flesh-digesting bacteria toxic to most other animals (Smithsonian Insider / Nature news)
Carcasses can carry pathogens like anthrax; vultures tolerate them and remove carcasses (TodayIFoundOut)
